title: Living Things
description: Biology from noticing living and non-living things to life cycles, classification, cells, human and plant systems, genetics and evolution. Emphasis on observation, fair testing and evidence.

Know that living things need food, water and air

lessons.title: Living or Not Living?
objectives: Sort things into living and non-living
Name things all living things need
prerequisites: Can name common animals and objects
explanation: Living things grow, need food and water, breathe air, and can have babies or make seeds. Animals, plants and people are living things.
Non-living things do not grow by themselves, eat or breathe. A rock, a toy car and a spoon are non-living.
Plants are alive too! They grow, drink water through their roots, and make seeds — even though they cannot walk.

vocabulary.meaning: alive: grows, needs food and water
not alive
get bigger over time
must have to stay alive

examples: A puppy grows into a dog — living.
A ball does not grow — non-living.

story.title: Kiko's Pet Rock
story.text: Kiko gave a rock some grass and water every day. "Grow, rock, grow!" But the rock stayed the same. Tara the tortoise smiled. "Rocks are not alive, Kiko. Let's plant a seed instead." A week later, a tiny green shoot appeared. "This one is alive!" Kiko cheered.

thinking: Is fire alive? It grows and needs air… what do you think?
Was a wooden table ever part of something living?
speaking: Find three living and three non-living things at home and explain how you decided.

project.title: Living and Non-Living Sorting Hunt
steps: Label one basket "living" and one "non-living"
Collect objects (use a photo or drawing for animals)
Sort them
Explain your trickiest choice

assessment.prompt: Which one can grow and needs water?
assessment.why: A sunflower is a living plant. It grows and takes in water through its roots.

assessment.prompt: A rock grows if you water it.

lessons.title: Baby Animals
objectives: Match baby animals to their adults
Describe how living things change as they grow
explanation: Animals have babies, called young. Many baby animals have special names: a baby cat is a kitten, a baby cow is a calf, a baby hen is a chick.
Some babies look like small adults, like puppies. Others look very different, like a caterpillar that becomes a butterfly, or a tadpole that becomes a frog.
You were a baby too! Now you are bigger, stronger, and can do many more things.

vocabulary.meaning: baby animals
a grown-up animal
get bigger
become different

examples: Calf → cow; kitten → cat.
Tadpole → frog: it grows legs and loses its tail.

story.title: Who Is My Mother?
story.text: A little duckling hatched and went looking for its mother. "Are you my mother?" it asked a cat. "No, I'm a cat. My babies are kittens." It asked a cow. "No, my baby is a calf." Then it heard "Quack!" — and there was Mother Duck, with more ducklings waddling behind.

activities.prompt: Some baby animals look very different from their parents.

thinking: Why do you think baby animals need their parents?
What can you do now that you could not do as a baby?
speaking: Look at a baby photo of yourself and tell someone three ways you have changed.

project.title: My Growing-Up Timeline
materials: photos or drawings of you at different ages
steps: Collect 3–4 photos or draw yourself as a baby, toddler and now
Stick them in order on a strip
Write or say one thing you could do at each age
Add a space for "when I grow up"

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Feathers, Fur and Fins
objectives: Sort animals into groups by their features
Describe the main features of each group
explanation: Scientists sort animals into groups by looking at their bodies. Mammals have hair or fur and feed their babies milk — like cows, elephants, dogs and humans.
Birds have feathers, beaks and lay eggs. Fish live in water, have fins and breathe with gills. Reptiles, like snakes and lizards, have dry scaly skin.
Amphibians, like frogs, live in water when young and on land as adults. Insects have six legs and three body parts — like ants, bees and butterflies.

vocabulary.meaning: an animal with hair that feeds its young milk
an animal with feathers and a beak
a small animal with six legs
a part or quality used to sort things

examples: A whale lives in water but is a mammal — it breathes air and feeds its baby milk.
A spider has eight legs, so it is not an insect.

story.title: The Bat's Problem
story.text: A bat flew to the birds' party. "You fly, so you're a bird!" they said. But the bat had fur, not feathers, and fed its babies milk. "I'm a mammal that flies!" the bat explained. The mammals cheered — and the birds let it stay for cake anyway.

activities.prompt: Match the animal to its group
How many legs does an insect have?

thinking: Why isn't a bat a bird, even though it flies?
Is a penguin a bird even though it cannot fly?
speaking: Choose an animal and explain to someone which group it belongs to and why.

project.title: Animal Group Sorting Cards
steps: Make a card for each animal
Sort them into mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, amphibians and insects
Check tricky ones (bat, whale, penguin, spider)
Make a poster of your groups

mastery: Classifies common animals into major groups

revision.notes: Short playful recall: replay activities, retell in own words, spot the idea in daily life.

lessons.title: Every Part Has a Job
objectives: Name the main parts of a plant
Explain the job of each part
explanation: Roots hold the plant in the ground and drink water from the soil. The stem holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves, like a straw.
Leaves catch sunlight to make food for the plant. Flowers make seeds, and often a fruit grows around the seeds to protect them.
Seeds can grow into new plants. That's why we find seeds inside mangoes, tomatoes and watermelons!

vocabulary.meaning: the part underground that takes in water
the part that holds the plant up
the part that makes food using sunlight
the part that can grow into a new plant

examples: We eat roots (carrots), stems (sugarcane), leaves (spinach), flowers (cauliflower), fruits (mango), seeds (peas).
A tree trunk is a very thick stem.

story.title: The Plant Team
story.text: Inside a sunflower, the parts were talking. "I drink water!" said Root. "I carry it up!" said Stem. "I make food from sunlight!" said Leaf. "I make seeds for new sunflowers!" said Flower. "We're a team," they agreed, "and nobody can do it alone."

activities.prompt: Match the part to its job
A tree trunk is a stem.

thinking: What would happen to a plant with no roots?
Why do you think many fruits taste sweet?
speaking: Show someone a real plant and point to each part, explaining its job.

project.title: Colour-Changing Celery
materials: a celery stick or white flower
steps: Put water and food colouring in a glass
Stand the celery or flower in it
Check after a few hours and the next day
Explain what the stem did
project.safety: Use a sturdy plastic cup instead of glass. Do not drink the coloured water or eat the celery after the experiment; wash hands afterwards.

assessment.prompt: Roots help hold a plant in the ground.

mastery: Names plant parts and their functions

units.title: Life Cycles
units.summary: Living things go through stages from birth to adult.
objectives: Describe the stages of a butterfly's life cycle
Compare complete metamorphosis with growth in mammals
masteryCriteria: Sequences life cycles of butterfly, frog and flowering plant

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: The Amazing Butterfly
objectives: Describe the stages of a butterfly's life cycle
Compare complete metamorphosis with growth in mammals
explanation: A butterfly's life is a cycle with four stages. It starts as a tiny egg laid on a leaf. A caterpillar (larva) hatches and eats and eats, growing quickly.
Then the caterpillar forms a chrysalis (pupa). Inside, its body is completely rebuilt. Finally, an adult butterfly comes out, and the adult lays eggs — and the cycle begins again.
This big change is called metamorphosis. Mammals don't do this: a kitten already looks like a small cat and simply grows.

vocabulary.meaning: the stages a living thing goes through, repeating each generation
the young stage, like a caterpillar
the resting stage when the body changes
a big change in body form

examples: Egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly.
Frogspawn → tadpole → froglet → frog.

story.title: The Very Hungry Caterpillar Inspector
story.text: Rangi found a striped caterpillar munching a milkweed leaf. Day after day it grew bigger. One morning, it hung upside down and turned into a green chrysalis. Rangi waited patiently for two weeks. Then — crack! — a wet, crumpled butterfly crawled out, dried its wings, and flew away.

activities.prompt: What does the caterpillar mainly do?
How many stages in a butterfly's life cycle?

thinking: Why is it called a cycle and not a line?
Why might a caterpillar need to eat so much?
speaking: Explain the butterfly life cycle to someone using hand actions for each stage.

project.title: Life Cycle Paper Plate
steps: Divide a plate into four sections
Draw or make each stage (rice for eggs, spiral pasta for caterpillar, shell pasta for chrysalis, bow pasta for butterfly)
Add arrows showing the cycle
Present it to your family

assessment.prompt: The big change in body form is called…

mastery: Sequences life cycles of butterfly, frog and flowering plant

units.title: Who Eats What?
units.summary: Energy passes from plants to animals in food chains.
objectives: Build a food chain starting with a plant
Classify animals as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores
masteryCriteria: Predicts effects of changes in a chain

revision.notes: Mixed recall: answer without looking back, explain to a family member, then re-check weak items.

lessons.title: Building a Food Chain
objectives: Build a food chain starting with a plant
Classify animals as herbivores, carnivores or omnivores
prerequisites: Knows plants make food from sunlight
explanation: Plants make their own food using sunlight, so they are called producers. Animals cannot make food; they eat plants or other animals, so they are consumers.
Herbivores eat plants (deer, cows). Carnivores eat other animals (tigers, eagles). Omnivores eat both (bears, crows, most humans).
A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows pointing to the eater: grass → deer → tiger. The arrow means "is eaten by" — energy flows along it.

vocabulary.meaning: a living thing that makes its own food (plants)
a living thing that eats others
eats only plants
eats other animals
eats plants and animals

examples: Leaves → caterpillar → sparrow → hawk.
Algae → small fish → kingfisher.

story.title: The Missing Grass
story.text: In a valley, the grass dried up in a long drought. The deer had little to eat and grew fewer. Then the tigers found fewer deer. When the rains returned and the grass grew, the deer returned, and so did the tigers. "Everything in a food chain is connected," said Tara.

activities.prompt: Every food chain starts with a…
In a food chain, arrows point to the animal doing the eating.

thinking: What would happen to the tigers if all the grass disappeared?
Why do food chains almost always start with plants?
speaking: Tell someone a food chain from the sea or forest and explain what the arrows mean.

project.title: Food Chain Paper Links
steps: Write a living thing on each strip (start with a plant)
Link strips into a chain in order
Make two different chains
Join them where an animal appears in both to make a mini food web
project.safety: An adult should operate the stapler and check that staples are fully closed. Use glue as a safer alternative for younger children; keep loose staples away.

mastery: Predicts effects of changes in a chain

units.title: Adaptation
units.summary: Features that help living things survive where they live.
objectives: Explain how features help animals and plants survive in their habitat
Compare adaptations in different habitats
masteryCriteria: Links features to survival in specific habitats
Explains camouflage and other adaptations with examples

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: Built to Survive
objectives: Explain how features help animals and plants survive in their habitat
Compare adaptations in different habitats
explanation: An adaptation is a feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat. Camels have wide feet for sand, long eyelashes against dust, and can go a long time without drinking.
Polar bears have thick fur and a layer of fat (blubber) to stay warm. Cacti store water in thick stems and have spines instead of leaves to lose less water.
Camouflage helps animals hide: a tiger's stripes blend with tall grass. Adaptations develop over many generations — an individual animal can't grow them just because it wants to.

context.text: A camel's hump stores mainly fat, not water. The fat can be used for energy when food is scarce.

vocabulary.meaning: a feature that helps a living thing survive
the natural home of a living thing
colours or patterns that help hide
a thick layer of fat

examples: Duck: webbed feet for swimming.
Owl: big eyes for seeing at night.

story.title: The Desert Swap
story.text: In a dream, a polar bear and a camel swapped homes. The polar bear panted in the hot desert, its thick fur far too warm. The camel shivered on the ice, its wide feet slipping. They woke up and both laughed with relief. "Our bodies are made for our own homes," said the camel.

activities.prompt: Match the animal to its adaptation
A camel's hump is full of water.
Why do cacti have spines instead of wide leaves?

thinking: If the Arctic gets warmer, which adaptations might become less useful?
Why can't an animal choose to grow a new adaptation?
speaking: Invent an imaginary animal for a habitat of your choice and explain its adaptations.

project.title: Blubber Glove
steps: Fill one bag with shortening and place an empty bag inside it to make a "blubber glove"
Put one hand in the blubber glove and one in an empty bag
Dip both in ice water
Time how long each hand can stay comfortably
Explain the result

assessment.prompt: Webbed feet help a duck to…

units.title: Body Systems
objectives: Describe the path of food through the digestive system
Explain the job of each main organ

revision.notes: Retrieval first, then review notes; interleave with other units; apply in a new example.

lessons.title: The Journey of a Sandwich
objectives: Describe the path of food through the digestive system
Explain the job of each main organ
explanation: Digestion breaks food into tiny pieces the body can use. It starts in the mouth: teeth chew and saliva begins breaking food down.
Food travels down the oesophagus (food pipe) to the stomach, where it is churned and mixed with acid. Then it moves to the small intestine, where nutrients pass into the blood.
The large intestine absorbs water from what is left, and the waste leaves the body. The whole journey usually takes from about one to two days or more.

vocabulary.meaning: breaking food down so the body can use it
the tube from mouth to stomach
the long tube where nutrients and water are absorbed
a useful substance in food

examples: Chewing well helps digestion.
Fibre from fruit and vegetables helps food move through the intestines.

story.title: A Ladoo's Adventure
story.text: A ladoo was popped into Kiko's mouth. Crunch, crunch — the teeth broke it up and saliva made it soft. Whoosh, down the oesophagus! Splash into the stomach for a churn. Then a long, winding trip through the small intestine, where its goodness passed into Kiko's blood to give energy for climbing.

activities.prompt: Match the organ to its job
Nutrients pass into the blood mainly in the…

thinking: Why is it important to chew food well?
Why do you think the small intestine is so long?
speaking: Trace the path of food on your own body with your finger and explain each stop.

project.title: Digestion in a Bag
materials: a piece of bread or a cracker
steps: Put bread in a bag with water (saliva)
Squish it (chewing and stomach churning) and add orange juice (acid)
Pour it into a stocking over a tray and squeeze (intestines absorbing)
Explain each step

assessment.prompt: Which tube carries food to the stomach?
Water is mainly absorbed in the…
Saliva helps start breaking food down.

units.title: Cells: Building Blocks of Life
units.summary: All living things are made of cells.
objectives: Identify parts of plant and animal cells and their functions
Compare plant and animal cells
masteryCriteria: Describes the history of cell discovery accurately

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Inside a Cell
objectives: Identify parts of plant and animal cells and their functions
Compare plant and animal cells
prerequisites: Knows living things grow and need nutrients
explanation: All living things are made of cells — the smallest units of life. Some living things are a single cell; your body has trillions.
Animal and plant cells both have a cell membrane (controls what goes in and out), cytoplasm (where chemical reactions happen) and a nucleus (contains genetic instructions).
Plant cells also have a cell wall (for strength), chloroplasts (where photosynthesis makes food), and usually a large vacuole (stores sap).

context.text: Robert Hooke named "cells" in 1665 after observing cork; Antonie van Leeuwenhoek observed single-celled organisms in the 1670s; cell theory was formalised in the 1830s by Schleiden and Schwann.

vocabulary.meaning: the basic unit of life
the control centre containing genetic material
where photosynthesis happens in plant cells
a thin layer controlling what enters and leaves

examples: Onion skin cells under a microscope look like bricks — plant cells with walls.
Cheek cells are rounder — animal cells, no wall.

story.title: The Tiny Rooms in the Cork
story.text: In 1665, Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his microscope. He saw many tiny box-like spaces and thought they looked like the small rooms monks lived in, called cells. The name stuck — and opened a whole invisible world.

activities.prompt: Match the part to its job
Which is found ONLY in plant cells?
All living things are made of cells.

thinking: Why do animal cells not need cell walls?
How did the microscope change what people believed about life?
speaking: Explain to someone the differences between a plant and animal cell using a model or drawing.

project.title: Edible or Craft Cell Model
steps: Make a plant cell: bag (membrane) in a box (cell wall)
Add items for nucleus, chloroplasts, vacuole
Make an animal cell without the box and chloroplasts
Label and present both

assessment.prompt: The "control centre" of the cell is the…
Plant cells have a cell wall made mainly of…

mastery: Describes the history of cell discovery accurately

units.title: Inheritance and Variation
units.summary: Why offspring resemble — and differ from — their parents.
objectives: Distinguish inherited traits from acquired characteristics
Explain why offspring vary
masteryCriteria: Recognises interaction of genes and environment

revision.notes: Self-test, explain the reasoning aloud, connect to other subjects, and attempt a transfer problem.

lessons.title: Inherited or Acquired?
objectives: Distinguish inherited traits from acquired characteristics
Explain why offspring vary
explanation: Offspring inherit characteristics from their parents through genes, which are made of DNA and found in the nucleus of cells. Eye colour and blood group are strongly inherited.
Acquired characteristics come from experience or environment: a scar, a language you speak, or muscles from exercise. These are not passed on through genes.
Each parent passes on half of their genes in different combinations, so siblings vary. Most traits, like height, are influenced by both genes and environment.

vocabulary.meaning: receive from parents
a section of DNA that influences a trait
differences between individuals
a trait developed during life, not inherited

examples: Inherited: natural hair colour. Acquired: dyed hair.
Height depends on genes AND nutrition.

story.title: The Gardener's Peas
story.text: In the 1860s, a monk named Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants and carefully counted tall and short, smooth and wrinkled peas over generations. His patient counting revealed patterns of inheritance — though the world mostly ignored his work until 1900.

activities.prompt: Siblings from the same parents always look identical.

thinking: If a weightlifter builds big muscles, will their children be born with big muscles? Why?
Why are identical twins useful for scientists studying genes and environment?
speaking: Explain to someone one trait you inherited and one you acquired.

project.title: Family Trait Survey
steps: Choose traits like earlobe shape, tongue rolling, dimples
Survey family members across generations
Record the results
Discuss patterns — and note that many traits are more complex than single genes
project.safety: Participation must be voluntary. Do not pressure relatives to share personal traits, label anyone, or infer health or genetic conditions; use fictional examples if anyone is uncomfortable.

assessment.prompt: Each parent passes on about half their genes.

mastery: Recognises interaction of genes and environment

stages.overview: Evolution by natural selection, genetics, and ecology at depth.
goals: Explain evolution by natural selection with evidence

units.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
objectives: Explain the mechanism of natural selection
Evaluate evidence for evolution
masteryCriteria: Explains natural selection clearly with examples
Distinguishes scientific explanation from belief respectfully

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Natural Selection
objectives: Explain the mechanism of natural selection
Evaluate evidence for evolution
explanation: Natural selection works through four observations: individuals vary; variations are inherited; more offspring are born than can survive; and those with helpful variations are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those variations on.
Over many generations, helpful traits become more common in a population. This is evolution. Individuals do not evolve; populations do.

Evidence includes the fossil record, similarities in bone structure between species (comparative anatomy), DNA comparisons, and evolution observed today, such as bacteria evolving antibiotic resistance.

context.text: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently proposed natural selection; their ideas were presented together in 1858, and Darwin published "On the Origin of Species" in 1859. Evolution is the central unifying theory of modern biology.

Some religious traditions interpret scientific evolution as compatible with their beliefs; some do not. Science describes natural processes and evidence; questions of ultimate meaning are explored in philosophy and religion.

vocabulary.meaning: the process where better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce more
change in inherited characteristics of a population over generations
preserved remains or traces of ancient life
bacteria surviving drugs meant to kill them

examples: Peppered moths in industrial England: darker forms became more common when trees were blackened by soot.
Antibiotic overuse selects for resistant bacteria.

story.title: Darwin's Finches
story.text: On the Galápagos Islands, Darwin collected birds with differently shaped beaks. Later studies by Peter and Rosemary Grant measured finches for decades: after a drought, birds with larger beaks that could crack tough seeds survived better, and the next generation had larger beaks on average.

activities.prompt: Order the logic of natural selection
An individual giraffe can stretch its neck and pass a longer neck to its babies.
activities.why: Acquired changes are not inherited; selection acts on inherited variation.

activities.prompt: Antibiotic resistance increases when antibiotics are…

thinking: Why does it matter to finish a course of antibiotics as prescribed?
Why do scientists say populations, not individuals, evolve?
speaking: Explain natural selection to someone using a simulation you design.

project.title: Beak Simulation

Collect food for 30 seconds per round
The least successful beaks "die" and others "reproduce"
Change the food type and repeat

project.safety: Use large, clean pretend food pieces that cannot be swallowed; do not use small beans or marbles with young children. Keep tools away from faces and do not harm real animals.

assessment.prompt: "On the Origin of Species" was published in…

mastery: Explains natural selection clearly with examples

units.title: Genetics
units.summary: Genes, alleles and patterns of inheritance.
objectives: Use Punnett squares to predict inheritance
Discuss ethical questions in genetics
masteryCriteria: Discusses genetic ethics with balanced reasoning

revision.notes: Spaced retrieval with written explanations, peer-teaching, and an extension question each cycle.

lessons.title: Punnett Squares
objectives: Use Punnett squares to predict inheritance
Discuss ethical questions in genetics
explanation: Genes come in versions called alleles. You inherit one allele of each gene from each parent. A dominant allele (written with a capital letter, e.g. B) shows its effect even if only one copy is present; a recessive allele (b) shows only if both copies are recessive.
A Punnett square predicts offspring probabilities. Two parents Bb × Bb produce BB, Bb, Bb, bb: a 3 in 4 chance of showing the dominant trait and 1 in 4 of the recessive trait.

Most human traits involve many genes and the environment, so simple Punnett squares apply only to some traits (such as some genetic conditions). Modern tools like CRISPR allow gene editing, raising important ethical questions.

context.text: DNA's double-helix structure was described in 1953 by Watson and Crick, using X-ray data produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins' teams.

vocabulary.meaning: a version of a gene
an allele expressed with one copy
an allele expressed only with two copies
the alleles an organism has
the observable characteristics

examples: Pea plants: tall (T) dominant over short (t). Tt × tt → 50% tall, 50% short.
Sickle cell trait follows recessive inheritance.

story.title: Franklin's Photograph 51
story.text: In the early 1950s, Rosalind Franklin captured a famous X-ray image of DNA, known as Photograph 51. It provided key evidence for the double-helix structure. Her contribution was under-recognised for many years — a reminder that science is the work of many people.

activities.prompt: An organism with alleles Tt shows which trait (T dominant)?
Most human traits are controlled by a single gene.

thinking: Should parents be allowed to choose traits for their children? Where would you draw the line?
Why was Rosalind Franklin's contribution overlooked?
speaking: Hold a short debate on one ethical question in genetic engineering, presenting both sides fairly.

project.title: Coin-Toss Genetics
steps: Label coins as Bb parents
Toss both coins 40 times to make "offspring"
Record genotypes
Compare ratios with the Punnett square prediction

assessment.prompt: Tt × tt offspring: % showing recessive trait?
Punnett squares give probabilities, not certainties.

mastery: Discusses genetic ethics with balanced reasoning
